Book
b'ook
n. (rendering Hebrew sepher, Greek biblion)
From Saxon boc, a book, and also a beech tree, from the beechen boards on which the northern nations cut their letters. Hebrew sepher is anything written — a letter, a deed of sale, a scroll of the law — from saphar, to count, to recount, to number; the same root gives the word for scribe. What is written is what has been counted, and what has been counted is not lost.

Biblical Definition

A book in Scripture is a written thing that outlasts the man who wrote it, and the Bible's own claim is that God keeps books. Moses, pleading for a rebellious nation, appeals to one: “Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin—; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exodus 32:32). David finds his own unformed body already entered in another: “in thy book all my members were written” (Psalm 139:16). A third is opened in a day when the faithful feared they had spoken to no purpose: “a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD” (Malachi 3:16). And the last vision of Scripture sets the books against the book: “the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life” (Revelation 20:12) — the record of works that condemns every man, and the register of grace that saves the elect. The word therefore carries two offices at once. It is the ordinary furniture of literate men, the deed and the letter and the scroll; and it is the figure under which God declares that nothing is forgotten, neither the sin He must judge nor the name He has written down in mercy. To have a book is to have a permanence that memory cannot supply, and that is exactly why God gave His church a book and not a tradition of talk.

Webster 1828 Definition

A written or printed volume; anything committed to writing and preserved; in Scripture, the roll of the law, the register of a man's days, the book of remembrance kept for them that fear the LORD, and the book of life in which the names of the redeemed are written.

expand to see more

BOOK, n. 1. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound.

2. A particular part of a literary composition; a division of a subject in the same volume.

3. A volume or collection of sheets in which accounts are kept; a register of debts and credits.

4. From Saxon boc, a beech tree, the bark or boards of which were used by the northern nations for writing.

5. In Scripture, the book of the law, Deut. 31; the book of life, Rev. 20; a book of remembrance, Mal. 3.

Key Scripture

Exodus 32:32 — "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin--; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written."

Psalm 139:16 — "Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them."

Malachi 3:16 — "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name."

Revelation 20:12 — "And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works."

Modern Corruption

The book of life is emptied of its particularity and treated as a register of all mankind, or as a roll a man may write himself into and out of at will; and the written word itself is demoted beneath the living voice of the church or of private impression.

expand to see more

The book of life is the first casualty. Universalist readings make it a roll of the whole race, so that Revelation 20:15 threatens no one; Arminian readings make it a list from which names are entered and erased with the fluctuations of a man's will, so that God's writing is only a record of ours. Scripture will bear neither. The names in it were written from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8), which is election in the plainest words the Spirit could use, and they were written by God, who does not learn and does not revise. Moses' plea in Exodus 32:32 is not a proof that names fall out of it but the intercession of a mediator offering himself in the place of the guilty — a shadow of the greater Mediator who was in fact blotted out of the land of the living for His people, that not one of theirs might be.

The second corruption is older and broader: the demotion of the written word beneath the unwritten. Rome sets an oral tradition beside the book and gives the magisterium the power to declare what the book means, so that in practice the book is read through the church rather than the church judged by the book. The charismatic wing of Protestantism does the same by another road, setting fresh impressions and prophecies beside the closed canon. Both forget why God gave a book at all. Speech dies with the speaker and is remembered as the hearer chooses; writing stands, is public, can be searched, and can convict the man who taught wrongly. That is why the Bereans could test an apostle, and why the LORD commanded the king to have his own copy in his own hand. A church that will not be judged by a book has arranged to be judged by nobody.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sepher, a writing, letter, or scroll, from saphar, to count or recount; Greek biblion, a small roll, from biblos, the papyrus pith on which men wrote.

expand to see more

Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a written document of any kind: a bill of divorcement, a deed, a letter, the book of the law; over 180 occurrences.

Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to count, number, recount, declare; the root behind both sepher, a book, and sopher, a scribe.

Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll or volume; the roll Jehoiakim cut with the penknife and burned (Jeremiah 36:23).

Greek biblion (G975) — a small book or scroll; the book of life, and the little book John was given to eat (Revelation 10:9).

Greek biblos (G976) — the inner bark of the papyrus, hence a written scroll; “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1).

Usage

"Of the divine register of the redeemed: another book was opened, which is the book of life (Revelation 20:12)."

"Of God's knowledge of a man before his birth: in thy book all my members were written (Psalm 139:16)."

"Of the LORD's notice of quiet fidelity: a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD (Malachi 3:16)."
